extraction.document_type: Theoretical computer science paper (working or conference version; no venue stated in the text)
extraction.identification: Not applicable: proof-based theory paper with no causal or empirical identification strategy.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (lines 0-299 and 300-745 of the text file, 29217 chars, under the 400000 limit). Covers front matter, abstract, introduction, Sections 2-7, Appendices A-D and references. Paul markup: none (p.annot_sha12s is empty and n_annots is 0); this is not one of Paul's own research notes. extraction.research_question: How can the linear threshold model of influence diffusion be extended to two competing technologies so that a player can choose early adopters to maximize its own spread, and does the greedy (1-1/e) approximation for influence maximization still apply to these competitive extensions?
extraction.theory: Extends the Kempe-Kleinberg-Tardos linear threshold model with competition. Four variants are proposed: a weight-proportional model where active neighbours of either technology share one threshold and adoption is split by weight; a separated-threshold model with technology-specific weights and thresholds; a forcing extension in which remaining inactive nodes adopt a technology at a final step; and an OR model where each technology spreads independently and a decision function chooses between them at the end, with a repeated-OR variant. Key properties studied are monotonicity and submodularity of the expected A-spread, which determine whether the Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher greedy guarantee applies.
extraction.data: No empirical data. Theoretical instances: directed graph G=(V,E) with per-technology edge weights in [0,1] whose incoming weights sum to at most 1, initial adopter sets for A and B, a budget k, and node thresholds drawn uniformly from [0,1] (or intervals). Sample sizes are illustrative trees and graphs in Figures 1-2 (for example a 7-node tree for the monotonicity counterexample). The hardness reduction builds a graph with N = O(n^(2 alpha+2)) nodes from a Vertex Cover instance.
extraction.method: Formal model definitions; monotonicity and submodularity counterexamples on small trees (Theorems 1-2, 4, 6; Appendices A, C); an inductive coupling proof over fixed thresholds and coin flips for monotonicity of the separated-threshold model (Lemma 3, Theorem 3, Appendix B); a live-edge equivalence argument for submodularity of the OR model (Lemma 2); a reduction from Vertex Cover for NP-hardness of approximation (Theorems 7-8, Appendix D); and application of Mossel-Roch's result for generalized submodular thresholds (Theorems 10-11).
extraction.scope: Abstract directed weighted social networks of arbitrary size; no population, institution or era. Main text uses two competing technologies, with a claim (no proof given) that results extend to several. Time is discrete steps with no calendar period. Results are worst-case or existence statements, not average-case.
measures: Expected number of A-active nodes sigma(IA, IB) at termination
Per-node activation probabilities alpha and beta at step t, and their values after adding a seed x
Monotonicity and submodularity of sigma
Approximation ratio under polynomial-time algorithms

summary_md: Borodin, Filmus and Oren (University of Toronto; no year or venue in the text, references run to 2010) ask whether the Kempe-Kleinberg-Tardos linear threshold model can be extended to two competing technologies while keeping the greedy (1-1/e) seed-selection guarantee. Mostly it cannot. A weight-proportional model, where an activated node adopts A with probability equal to A's share of active incoming weight, is not even monotone: adding an A seed moves a root's A-probability from 11/40 to 103/400. A separated-threshold model with per-technology weights and thresholds is monotone but not submodular, and adding a forcing step does not fix this under any tie-breaking rule. With technology-specific weights, the follower problem is NP-hard to approximate within Omega(N^(1/2-eps)). The same reduction refutes a Carnes et al. conjecture. Only the OR model, where each technology spreads independently and a monotone submodular decision function picks the winner at the end, keeps the greedy guarantee, including repeated rounds. For the system as built, the paper is already cited (scenario.py, write_im_sheet.py) as the reason the FLIP side carries no guarantee. That citation is broadly right but loosely mapped. FLIP's pflip = a/(a+b) has the same form as Borodin's weight-proportional adoption split, but it has no random thresholds and no propagation. In a fixed stance state it is separable and concave, so the optimizer's exact certificate holds. The paper bites in two places: modeled-conversion replanning, where the max-normalized neighbour term can make adding pro mass lower other members' pflip, and the coalition frontier's lazy greedy. The frontier keeps one shared kernel for both colours, which stays clear of the Theorem 8 hardness, but its objective includes contest seeds, the seed gate and the leverage factor, and nothing proves those submodular. All bearings below are UNVERIFIED agent analysis (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: In the weight-proportional competitive LT model (Eq. 1) the A-spread is not monotone (Theorem 1: root A-probability 11/40 before and 103/400 after adding one A seed, Appendix A Theorem 12) and not submodular (Theorem 2). The Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher greedy bound does not transfer to that model.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2, Eq. 1, Theorems 1-2; Appendix A Theorems 12-13, Figure 1
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b) (flip_model.py 92-97) has the form of Eq. 1, but a and b each add a money term to WP*nA/mAt, so it is not the same model. Stance is fixed inside a run, so the objective is separable by member. optimize.py checks concavity at run time (concavity_violations) and labels only the fixed-state run as fixed_state_lazy_greedy. A modeled conversion re-runs topic_setup, where mAt = max(nA) (flip_model.py 138-140), so one conversion can lower another member's WP*nA/mAt term. Such a run is labeled modeled_threshold_replanning (optimize.py 190) and carries no certificate.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Structural analogy only. Borodin non-monotonicity runs through multi-step propagation under random thresholds, which pflip does not have. The conversion-path concern applies only when conversion_reachable is true. Whether the mAt renormalisation lowers total winnability after a conversion is not measured in this text.

The analyst called the fixed-state objective concave; the code only tests concavity at run time and the docstring asserts diminishing returns, so the wording is now checked, not proven. The Eq. 1 match is partial because the money term is absent from Borodin model.

meta.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility

extraction.title: The Effect of Politicians' Personality on Their Media Visibility
extraction.document_type: Empirical journal article: elite survey (Big Five via TIPI) linked to news-mention counts, cross-sectional OLS
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1253 lines of the text file (front matter, abstract, introduction, theory, hypotheses, method, measures, controls, results, Table 1, robustness, discussion, limitations, notes, references, author bios). Online Appendices A-E are cited in the text but are not in the file, so their contents (summary statistics, parsimonious models, randomization inference, country-level and Belgian parliament-level models) are not covered. Paul's markup: none supplied (the task listed no markup files).
extraction.research_question: Do politicians' Big Five personality traits predict how often they are covered in national news media, beyond institutional power and other individual-level explanations (political power, activity, communication skill, demographics)? The paper focuses on agreeableness and extraversion as interpersonal traits, and also tests openness, neuroticism and conscientiousness (pp. 2-3, lines 74-78 and 146-156).
extraction.theory: Two mechanisms link traits to visibility (pp. 5-6). (1) A motivational mechanism: traits shape need for interaction and attention, so some politicians seek coverage more (cites Costa & McCrae 1988; Mondak 2010; Cohen et al. 2008; Sheafer 2001). (2) A news-values mechanism: traits shape behaviours that fit journalistic selection criteria (camera performance, sound bites, surprising initiatives) and the ability to cultivate journalist relationships. The authors argue newsworthiness matters more than journalist relationships when the two conflict (p. 7; Helfer & Van Aelst 2016). Agreeableness and extraversion are the most interpersonal traits and voters rely on them (pp. 5-6; Caprara et al. 2002). Hypotheses: H1 agreeableness negative; H2 extraversion positive; H3 openness positive; H4 neuroticism negative; H5 conscientiousness positive (pp. 8-10).
extraction.data: Unit: incumbent member of parliament (MP). Survey sample N = 339 MPs in three countries, fielded March to August 2015 (p. 10). Belgium: 95 federal MPs (54th federal parliament) and 139 regional MPs, 57% response rate. Canada: 45 federal MPs (41st parliament) and 28 Ontario provincial MPs, 26% response rate (278 contacted). Israel: 32 MPs (20th Knesset), 27% response rate (p. 10 and note 1, p. 20). Media counting windows (note 3, p. 21): Canada federal June 2, 2011 to Aug 2, 2015; Ontario July 2, 2014 to Dec 31, 2015; Belgium June 19, 2014 to Nov 30, 2015; Israel Mar 31 to Dec 31, 2015. Media outlets (p. 10): Belgium 6 newspapers, 2 news websites, 2 TV channels; Canada 3 newspapers, 2 websites, 1 TV channel (CTV); Israel 2 newspapers, 2 websites, 2 TV channels. Regression N: Model 1 n = 306; Model 2 (newspapers) n = 296; Model 3 (websites) n = 286; Model 4 (TV) n = 174 (Table 1, p. 14). The text does not explain why Model 1 n is 306 rather than 339.
extraction.method: Dependent variable: count of mentions of each MP's full name in each country's major outlets, rescaled per country and medium to 0-1 (min-max, note 4), summed and rescaled again to 0-1 (M = .08, SD = .14, skewness 3.77). Log-transformed for OLS (p. 13); note 11 gives an alternative that adds half the smallest nonzero value. Personality: 10-item TIPI (Gosling et al. 2003), 7-point scale, two items per trait, reverse-coded where needed, averaged per trait (pp. 11-12). Main model: multivariate OLS with standardized betas on all five traits plus controls. Robustness: separate OLS models by medium (Models 2-4); a parsimonious demographic-only model and per-country parsimonious models (Online Appendix E); a randomization inference test (Malesky et al. 2014) for joint significance (pp. 16-17). Controls (pp. 12-13): gender, age, parliamentary experience, coalition membership, minister, party leader, house speaker, conservatism (binary), federal vs regional MP, parliamentary activity (standardized counts of bills, questions, etc.), Facebook posts (standardized), country dummies. Note 10: VIF below 1.63.
extraction.identification: None beyond covariate adjustment. The design is a single-wave cross-sectional survey linked to media counts, analysed with OLS controlling for institutional power, activity, communication effort, demographics, ideology and country. The paper does not use an instrument, panel, experiment or natural variation. The title's "effect" is the authors' framing of conditional associations. Robustness is by medium, by country, by a parsimonious specification, and by randomization inference.
extraction.scope: Population: incumbent MPs and provincial/regional members in Belgium, Canada (federal and Ontario) and Israel, sampled during the 2011-2015 legislatures. Institutions: three developed parliamentary democracies with different electoral systems (Canada single-member plurality; Belgium multimember with 11 districts; Israel one national proportional district) (pp. 9-10). Era: media coverage counted over roughly 2011-2015, depending on country. The authors say findings may extend to other developed democracies, but they do not claim generalization to presidential or nondemocratic systems (p. 19).

key_findings.finding: H1 supported: agreeableness is negatively associated with national media visibility (less agreeable MPs covered more).
key_findings.location: Results p. 13; Table 1 Model 1 p. 14; Discussion p. 17
key_findings.numbers: b = -0.184 (SE 0.075), standardized beta = -.116, p < .05

key_findings.finding: H2 supported: extraversion is positively associated with national media visibility.
H3 supported: openness to experience is positively associated with visibility.
H4 supported: neuroticism (emotional instability) is negatively associated with visibility; more emotionally stable MPs are covered more.
H5 not supported in the pooled model: conscientiousness has a near-zero, insignificant association with visibility.

Institutional power dominates. Being a minister has the largest standardized effect. The personality effects are about one-third as large, and a party leader's effect is only slightly larger than the personality effects.
key_findings.numbers: Minister beta = .369 (b = 3.122, p < .001); party leader beta = .195 (b = 1.836, p < .001); house speaker not significant; overall R2 = .483

key_findings.finding: Medium-specific robustness. Newspapers: agreeableness b = -0.243 (p < .01), extraversion and neuroticism significant at p < .1, openness and conscientiousness not significant. Websites: extraversion (b = 0.117, p < .05), openness (b = 0.230, p < .01) and neuroticism (b = -0.191, p < .01) significant; agreeableness negative but not significant (-0.102); conscientiousness not significant. TV (n = 174): agreeableness (-0.188) and extraversion (0.128) at p < .1; other traits not significant.
key_findings.location: Robustness Checks pp. 15-16; Table 1 Models 2-4 p. 14

key_findings.finding: Conscientiousness is positive and significant in Canada and Israel but not in Belgium. The authors attribute the Belgian null partly to TIPI measurement error (attenuation). Among Belgian regional MPs (n = 137) conscientiousness significantly decreases visibility; the federal Belgian effect (n = 95) is not significant.
key_findings.location: Robustness pp. 17-18; Discussion pp. 18 (lines 917-935); per-country and Belgian-parliament detail in Online Appendix E
key_findings.numbers: Per-country samples: Israel n = 32, Belgium n = 234 (95 federal + 139 regional), Canada n = 73 (45 federal + 28 Ontario); the country-level coefficients are not reported in the main text

key_findings.finding: Authors read the results as personality having a substantial effect beyond institutional explanations, with traits that fit news values (extraversion) giving a long-lasting advantage.
key_findings.numbers: Four of five traits significant in the pooled model; one trait (conscientiousness) partly predicts (abstract p. 1; discussion p. 18)

measures: Media visibility: outlet-level counts of full-name mentions (newspapers via LexisNexis or outlet sites; TV transcripts or manual broadcast counts; website unique articles), manually checked for the right person; rescaled 0-1 per country and medium; summed and rescaled again (note 2 p. 20; p. 10-11).

Big Five: 10-item TIPI (Gosling, Rentfrow & Swann 2003), English version and Dutch, French and Hebrew translations; 7-point agree/disagree; two items per trait; averaged per trait. Inter-item r: extraversion .61, openness .25, neuroticism .37, conscientiousness .29, agreeableness .09 (ns). Cronbach alpha: extraversion .75, openness .39, neuroticism .53, conscientiousness .40, agreeableness .15 (note 7 p. 21). Only extraversion had an eigenvalue above 1 (p. 12).
Parliamentary power: dummies for minister, party leader, house speaker.
Parliamentary activity: count of bills initiated, questions, laws passed, motions, etc., varying by parliament (note 8 p. 21), standardized 0-1 within each parliament.
Facebook posts: count from public pages (Facepager) or manual count, standardized 0-1 within country (note 9 p. 21).
Ideology: binary conservatism (Chapel Hill Expert Survey for Belgium; Conservative Party for Canada; Hazan & Diskin 2015 classification for Israel).
Demographics: gender, age, years since first election, coalition membership, federal vs regional parliament, country dummies.
limitations: Social desirability: self-reported personality from office holders may be biased, e.g. understated irritability and overstated dependability (p. 19).

Brief TIPI measure with low reliability, especially agreeableness (alpha .15; r = .09, ns). The authors say this likely underestimates true effects (pp. 11-12, 19; note 7 p. 21). Facet-level effects cannot be separated (p. 19).
Only three countries, so generalization to presidential or nondemocratic systems is not established (p. 19-20).
Small national subsamples (Israel n = 32) limit the country-level conclusions, particularly for conscientiousness (pp. 17-18).
Only visibility (volume) is measured, not tone of coverage (p. 20).
The two proposed mechanisms (motivation and newsworthiness) are not measured directly and cannot be disentangled (p. 20).
Low response rates (Canada 26%, Israel 27%; Belgium 57%) and unexplained drop from N = 339 to n = 306 in Model 1 (pp. 10, 13-14).
Cross-sectional design with media counts over different windows across countries, so no causal or temporal ordering is established beyond the covariate-adjusted association (note 4, p. 21).

Politicians high on these traits, we argue, enjoy an inherent advantage in the competition for the media's attention.

summary_md:
Amsalem, Zoizner, Sheafer, Walgrave and Loewen (2018) linked a 2015 elite survey of 339 legislators in Belgium, Canada (federal and Ontario) and Israel to counts of how often each was named in national newspapers, news websites and TV. Personality was measured with the 10-item TIPI. Window: media counted over country-specific periods between 2011 and 2015. Denominator: n = 306 in the pooled model.

In a pooled cross-sectional OLS with country dummies, four traits predict visibility, each with a standardized beta of about 0.1:
- extraversion: positive (beta .117)
- agreeableness: negative (-.116)
- neuroticism: negative (-.111)
- openness: positive (.098)

Conscientiousness is null in the pooled model and splits by country. Office matters far more: being a minister has beta .369 and being a party leader .195, with R² = .483. The measures are weak. Agreeableness has alpha .15 and its two items correlate at only r = .09 (not significant). Response rates are 26-57%. The paper does not identify a causal effect, so its "effect" is a covariate-adjusted association.

For Melange the paper matters in three places:
1. The behavioural visibility disposition is counted from interviews and labelled extraversion-sociability. The paper's extraversion result supports that label, but the paper also shows visibility loads on low agreeableness, emotional stability and, mostly, office.
2. That disposition raises seed_prob in the receptivity layer. The lexical susceptibility weights point the other way on agreeableness and neuroticism, so the two disagree.
3. Interview-derived traits, including affective N, exist only for members who get airtime. Everyone else is set to neutral. If airtime selects on temperament, as this paper finds, that missingness is not random.

None of this has been tested on US Congress data.

bearings.paper_claim: Extraversion is positive and significant in the pooled OLS: b = 0.129 (SE 0.052), beta .117, p < .05 (Model 1, n = 306, R2 = .483, country dummies and controls). Also significant on news websites (Model 3, b = 0.117, p < .05).

Office is the dominant predictor there, so a US interview count needs office controls before it reads as temperament. Conscientiousness flips by stratum (positive in Canada and Israel, null in Belgium, negative among Belgian regional MPs, n = 137). paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees in part with his stated positions. He treats a member's public statements as the observable persona (press-pillar) and wants psychological traits to adjust response to pressure (receptivity-layer). The paper supports the idea that public presence is shaped by temperament, but finds office drives it about three times as strongly. That argues for controlling for office before reading interview or press volume as a trait. His receptivity notes predate the behavioural basis. In the current code, visibility_z enters seed_prob, and the paper's trait profile for highly visible members (low A, low N) cuts against the lexical susceptibility weights. His Ramey citations (personality and legislative behaviour) are consistent with this paper's framework, and the paper cites Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh 2017 on cosponsorship.

meta.title: Is Bigger Always Better? Potential Biases of Big Data Derived from Social Network Sites
meta.venue: The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, vol. 659 (May 2015), pp. 63-76. Special issue: Big Data Methodological Challenges.

extraction.title: Is Bigger Always Better? Potential Biases of Big Data Derived from Social Network Sites
extraction.venue: The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, vol. 659 (May 2015), pp. 63-76. Special issue: Big Data Methodological Challenges.
extraction.document_type: Journal article; short essay with an empirical illustration (two survey datasets, logistic regressions)
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in one pass (abstract, introduction, sampling-frame discussion, both empirical sections, Tables 1-4, conclusion, notes, references). Paul's markup: none supplied, so paul_markup is empty. The text file is plain extracted text, so no highlights or sticky notes exist to recover.
extraction.research_question: Are people's choices to use specific social network sites (SNSs) random with respect to demographics, socioeconomic status and Internet experience? If not, can big data studies that sample only users of one SNS generalize their findings to the broader population or to users of other SNSs?
extraction.theory: No named theory. The argument rests on sampling-frame logic: a site's users are the sampling frame, non-users are excluded by design, and generalization requires that selection into the site be unrelated to the outcomes studied. The paper also invokes selection on the dependent variable as a second source of bias.
extraction.data:
Dataset 1 (national): Pew Internet Project survey collected 2013, N = 1,801 adults (80.2% use the Internet); landline and cellular random-digit-dial sample; average age 52, half male, 70% white. Regression N ranges 1,510-1,528 (full sample) and 1,231-1,249 (Internet users only), per Table 1.
Dataset 2 (panel): Author's panel of young adults at the University of Illinois at Chicago (UIC), a required first-year class. Wave 1 spring 2009, n = 547 (80.5% of enrolled students); wave 2 summer 2012 by postal mail, 52% of wave 1 returned valid responses. Regression N = 517-519 (Table 4). Group is 61% women, 44% white non-Hispanic, 24% Asian American, 23% Hispanic, 8% African American; ages 21-22 in 2012; 50% of parents have a college degree or more. Paper-pencil instruments in both waves.
extraction.method:
Separate logistic regressions for each SNS.
Pew analysis (Table 1): outcome is current use of Facebook, LinkedIn or Twitter (cross-sectional, 2013). Predictors: age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, logged income. Run on full sample and on Internet users only.
Panel analysis (Table 4): outcome is 2012 adoption of Facebook, Twitter, Google+, LinkedIn or Tumblr (MySpace dropped for low uptake). Predictors are 2009 measures: gender, race/ethnicity, parental education, logged use years, logged user autonomy (access locations), use frequency, and Internet skills. Internet skills index = mean of 27 Internet terms rated on a 5-point scale (Cronbach's alpha = .94). Descriptive usage trends are in Table 3.
extraction.identification: Temporal ordering only. Panel predictors are measured in 2009 and outcomes in 2012, so the author argues that skills and experiences predate most SNS adoption (Table 3 shows Twitter at 3% in 2009). This is offered as a partial answer to reverse causality from SNS use to skills. No instrument, experiment or quasi-experimental design is used. The Pew analysis is cross-sectional and carries no such ordering.
extraction.scope: Population: US adults (Pew, 2013) and a single-institution cohort of first-year students (UIC, 2009-2012, ages 21-22 in 2012). The panel is described as homogeneous on age and education, racially and socioeconomically diverse, and not a random sample of the national population. Era: 2009-2013, a period when Facebook was dominant and Twitter, Google+, LinkedIn and Tumblr were growing.

key_findings.finding: Adoption of Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter is not random with respect to demographics and SES in the national Pew data. Older people are less likely to use all three; the least educated and lower-income people are less likely to use all three.
key_findings.location: Pew results, Table 1 and text, pp. 67-68
key_findings.numbers: Age: Facebook -0.05, LinkedIn -0.02, Twitter -0.06 (all p < .001, full sample). Facebook high school or less: -0.61 (p < .001); LinkedIn: -1.37 (p < .001); Twitter: -0.56 (p < .01). LinkedIn income (logged): 0.72 (p < .001). Pattern largely holds among Internet users only. Shares: Facebook 53% of all adults (text says just over half, or two-thirds of Internet users); LinkedIn 19% of all, 24% of Internet users; Twitter 13% of all, 15% of Internet users. R-squared .09-.16.

key_findings.finding: Gender and race differ by site. Women are more likely on Facebook (+0.46) and less likely on LinkedIn (-0.39). Black respondents are more likely on LinkedIn and Twitter but less likely on Facebook.
key_findings.numbers: Female Facebook 0.46 (p < .001); female LinkedIn -0.39 (p < .01); Black Twitter 0.63 (p < .01); Black LinkedIn 0.68 (p < .01); Black Facebook -0.31 (p < .10 only).

key_findings.finding: In the young-adult panel, 2009 demographics predict 2012 SNS adoption for Twitter and Tumblr: women, African Americans and students with less-educated parents are more likely on Twitter, and women more likely on Tumblr. Asian Americans are less likely on LinkedIn.
key_findings.location: Panel results, Table 4 and text, pp. 72-73
key_findings.numbers: Female Tumblr 0.84 (p < .01); female Twitter 0.51 (p < .05); Black Twitter 0.87 (p < .05); high school or less parental education Twitter -0.85 (p < .01), Tumblr -1.08 (p < .01); Asian LinkedIn -0.29 (p < .10). Panel R-squared .03-.08.

key_findings.finding: Internet experience and skills predict later adoption. Higher use frequency predicts adoption of four of five sites (all except Twitter). Internet skills from 2009 predict Twitter, LinkedIn and Tumblr adoption in 2012.
key_findings.location: Panel results, Table 4 and text, pp. 72-73
key_findings.numbers: Use frequency: Facebook 0.48, Google+ 0.45, LinkedIn 0.52, Tumblr 0.48 (all p < .05). Internet skills: Twitter 0.33 (p < .05), LinkedIn 0.33 (p < .05), Tumblr 0.62 (p < .001). Skills not significant for Facebook (-0.06) or Google+ (0.22).

key_findings.finding: Adoption is low for most platforms even among this group, so no single SNS can serve as a representative sampling frame. Facebook is near-saturated while the others vary sharply.
key_findings.location: Panel usage, Table 3 and text, p. 71
key_findings.numbers: 2009 / 2012 adoption: Facebook 87% / 89%; Twitter 3% / 38%; LinkedIn 0% / 18%; Tumblr N/A / 16%; Google+ not launched / 22%; MySpace 36% / 2%. Text: Twitter used by 37.5% in 2012.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: SNS-derived log data are biased toward certain populations (demographics, SES, Internet skills, topical interest). Findings may be wrong in direction, not just imprecise. Good sampling must not be confounded with the substantive question, and studies must state their sampling-frame scope in titles, abstracts, methods, results and press communication.
key_findings.numbers: No new numbers; the conclusion reasons from Tables 1-4 and cites Hargittai (2011) on opposite-direction conclusions.

measures: SNS use (Pew 2013): current use of Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter (binary).
SNS adoption (UIC panel): 'ever used' item collapsed to current use ('sometimes' or 'often') for Facebook, MySpace, Twitter, Google+, LinkedIn, Tumblr.
Demographics: age, gender, race/ethnicity, education (Pew), parental education (panel), logged household income (Pew).
Internet experience: use years (logged), user autonomy as number of access locations (logged), use frequency (weekly web hours; lagged in panel).
Internet skills: mean of 27 Internet terms on a 5-point understanding scale; Cronbach's alpha = .94 (panel, validated instrument from Hargittai 2005, 2009; Hargittai and Hsieh 2012).
limitations: Author's stated limits: Pew did not disaggregate SNS use by service before 2012, did not measure Internet skills, and is cross-sectional with no repeated respondents.

Panel is one required class at one university (UIC), homogeneous on age and education, not a random sample, and only 547 cases; 52% retention to 2012, with African American share falling from 11% to 8%.
Paper-pencil surveys, chosen to avoid online-survey bias; the mode choice is a deliberate design decision, not a limitation the author fully resolves.
Analyses include one SNS at a time and do not control for use of other SNSs (note 3: 28% of Internet users in the Pew sample use more than one SNS; note 4: 56.4% in the panel).
Study covers only SNS use, not other platforms or offline ties; the Burke and Kraut example shows how single-platform data miss activity elsewhere (pp. 65-66).
Author limits the paper to one bias (single-SNS sampling frames) due to space constraints (p. 65).
Temporal ordering is a partial answer to reverse causality, not a causal design.

summary_md:
Hargittai asks whether people choose social network sites at random. They do not. In the 2013 Pew national survey (N = 1,801; regression N about 1,510-1,528), age, education, income, gender and race each predict use of Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter. For example, the LinkedIn coefficient on logged income is 0.72 and on high school or less is -1.37. In a panel of UIC students (2009 to 2012, regression N about 517-519), 2009 Internet skills and use frequency predict which sites people adopted by 2012 (skills to Tumblr 0.62, Twitter 0.33). Adoption differs widely by site (2012: Facebook 89%, Twitter 38%, LinkedIn 18%). Her conclusion is that data from one site describe that site's users only. A biased sampling frame can reverse the direction of a finding, not just add noise. Studies should state their frame in the title, abstract and results.

**What this means here.** Legislators are elite accounts, so platform adoption bias mostly disappears on X: 502 of 515 members in social_media.db have an X handle. It comes back on Bluesky. Bluesky posts run 2023-07-01 to 2026-09-19. Of the 533 roster members (259 D, 271 R, 3 I), 135 posted on Bluesky: 117 D, 16 R and 2 I. Of the 411 Bluesky member-to-member mentions, 392 are D to D, and none cross party. These mentions are added at weight 0.4 to the social interaction layer, which enters the live augmented cascade network. The second problem is the media blend: a member silent on social media in a category gets half their press signal, so silence counts as zero stance. Both counts are my own reading of live files. They stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062). The paper's coefficients do not carry over to this system. Only its sampling-frame logic does.

bearings.paper_claim: People do not select into SNS use at random, and selection differs by site and demographic group. Pew 2013 logistic coefficients (full sample, N 1,510 to 1,528, log-odds): female on Facebook 0.46 (p<.001), female on LinkedIn -0.39 (p<.01), Black on Twitter 0.63 (p<.01). Black on Facebook -0.31 is p<.10 only and -0.06 among Internet users, so it is not a reliable selection effect. Users of one platform are not the population.

bearings.system_side: social_interaction_layer.py: X reposts 1.0, X mentions 0.4, Bluesky mentions 0.4; pair p = events / max(25, X-post count of author), cap 0.25, so Bluesky events enter the numerator only (confirmed). build_multilayer_network.py: new edge w = 6p/(1-p) cap 2.0, or up to +30 percent reinforcement on existing ties (confirmed). Read-only counts from social_media.db on 2026-10-09: 411 Bluesky mentions = 392 D to D, 8 D to I, 5 I to D, 6 R to R, 0 D to R; 135 posters = 117 D, 16 R, 2 I; roster 533 = 259 D, 271 R, 3 I; posts 2023-07-01 to 2026-09-19. JSON written 2026-09-19 holds 739 pairs, 275 reposts, 953 mentions (X and Bluesky). Unverified: rows present at JSON write time, since the DB was modified 2026-10-04.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Her coefficients do not transfer; her frame logic may. Her data are US adults (2013) and one 2009-2012 student cohort, not legislators or Bluesky. That X adoption bias is mostly gone for legislators is the analyst's inference: the paper never discusses institutional accounts (502 of 515 member rows have an X handle, read-only). The Bluesky handle field is populated for all 515 rows, so 135 is posting, not account adoption. Party-skewed posting may carry a party-skewed edge pattern into the layer; untested, UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Counts and code confirmed exactly. Softened: (1) none cross party holds only for D vs R; 13 mentions cross the D/I line. (2) Black on Facebook is p<.10 only. (3) The X-adoption claim is analyst inference, not the paper's. (4) Denominators 515 (db) and 533 (roster) must be named at each figure.

bearings.paper_claim: Non-users are excluded from a site-based sampling frame by design. If selection is related to outcomes, results from users may reach the opposite conclusion about the wider population. Sampling should not be tied to the substantive question. The paper does not discuss how missing social-media activity should be coded.

bearings.system_side: build_media_blend.py: SOCIAL_W = 0.5; f = min(1, nz/15), with nz the members carrying a nonzero social value in the category (shrink on by default). Cell = (1 - 0.5f) x press/p80 + 0.5f x social/p80. A member with no social value gets sv = 0, so at f = 1 the press side is halved and silence scores as zero, not missing (confirmed at lines 29, 463, 479). The downstream Press Release - Raw link was not checked.

The concern bites only if posters differ from non-posters on stance in categories where f = 1; that is untested, and the analyst's own note says so. The stance-ladder rule on missing evidence was not checked. UNVERIFIED.

Registry figures (P(CU-relevant given CU title) 0.825 vs 0.0089; coverage D 92.5 vs R 87, Senate 83 vs House 96) match the component registry text; not re-measured from the corpus.

The cap is not party- or chamber-specific, so 'favours House and Democratic offices' does not follow from the code; it rests on unmeasured coverage rates. The collector comment assumes the skipped bulk is missing at random, which is the untested premise.

summary_issues: Overstated: 'age, education, income, gender and race each predict use of Facebook, LinkedIn and Twitter'. Gender is null for Twitter (-0.00), income is null for Facebook among Internet users (-0.12), and Hispanic is null for all three. Should say each predicts use of at least one site.
The 0.72 (LinkedIn, logged income) and -1.37 (LinkedIn, high school or less) are log-odds coefficients from the full Pew sample (N 1,510 for LinkedIn), not effect sizes. Name the scale and window.
'A biased sampling frame can reverse the direction of a finding' overstates the paper's 'may come to the exact opposite conclusion' (p. 74). Use 'may'.
'Legislators are elite accounts, so platform adoption bias mostly disappears on X' is the analyst's inference, not the paper's; the paper never discusses institutional accounts. Mark it as inference.
'none cross party' holds only for D vs R. The same paragraph's counts show 8 D to I and 5 I to D mentions; state that 13 cross the D/I line.

Denominators are mixed: 502 of 515 have an X handle (social_media.db members table, 515 rows) while party counts use the 533 roster. The Bluesky handle field is populated for all 515 rows, so 135 posters is posting, not account adoption. Name the denominator at each figure.

The UIC panel 2012 figures (Facebook 89, Twitter 38, LinkedIn 18 percent) come from a 2012 wave with 52 percent return and no N in Table 3; name that. 'UIC students' should read young adults in one required first-year class (2009 wave n = 547).
Paul-alignment claims (Fink framework; critiques on sign, third-party sentiment and temporal weighting) were not checked against his annotation files; treat as unverified.

Extraction issues in ext: the 'space constraints' limitation is on p. 66, not p. 65; Black on Facebook -0.31 and Asian on LinkedIn -0.29 need p<.10 flags; 'no single SNS can serve as a sampling frame' is the extractor's inference, while the paper says the usage rates should give pause (p. 71).

Coverage: all 3 bearings and all 4 related links checked; Tables 1, 3 and 4 re-read in the paper text; code ranges re-read; DB and roster counts re-derived read-only. Not checked: brain figures beyond component registry text, Paul's annotation claims beyond the Baptista highlight, and the 400 tweet-gold count.
gaps_exposed: The social layers carry no per-platform frame statement. social_interactions.json has a provenance string but no per-platform event counts or party mix, so the Bluesky D-skew is invisible downstream.

Volume normalization in the social layer uses an X-only post count as the denominator for events from X and Bluesky combined. Cross-platform activity is not on a common base. Any change here would need its own ruling; this is not a recommendation to normalize per edge.

The media blend treats social silence as zero stance rather than missing. No test checks whether non-posters differ systematically (party, chamber) from posters in the categories where the social share is fully on (f = 1).
Gold sets (400 tweet golds) and stance accuracy figures describe members who post. Their scope does not say that the accuracies cover only the posting population.
Press, social and Bluesky corpora have no published per-party and per-chamber coverage tables next to the pillar. Coverage figures live only in brain notes.
flags: UNVERIFIED (DE-062): the Bluesky party mix (135 posters: 117 D / 16 R / 2 I; 411 mentions: 392 D->D, 0 cross-party; window 2023-07-01 to 2026-09-19; denominator 533 roster members) is a single-path read of social_media.db joined to responsiveness_layers.json party. It needs a second path, and a check that these rows existed when social_interactions.json was built on 2026-09-19.

Not a call for per-edge volume normalization (REJECTED in this project). The code already applies per-author normalization; the issue raised is the mismatched X-only denominator and the unstated frame. Any fix must avoid re-proposing the rejected option.
Not a call to drop regular cosponsorship edges (REJECTED). Hargittai's argument concerns social-platform layers, not the cosponsor base.
Edge weights in this layer are heuristic model inputs, never closeness or access probabilities (D-025). A D-heavy Bluesky subgraph must not be described as Democrats being 'closer'.

The media blend scores social silence as zero, which sits awkwardly with the stance contract's stated rule that missing evidence is never imputed as neutral (category-stance-ladder assumption). Recorded as an observation for Paul to rule on, not a finding.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper. His positions on the affected components are Fink as the framework for the social layer, his critiques on sign, third-party sentiment and temporal weighting, and Baptista's highlighted caution that more layers are not always better. Hargittai supports the Baptista caution from a sampling angle that his notes do not raise: each added platform layer brings its own selected population. For legislators that shows up as party skew on Bluesky, not as the age, income or education skew Hargittai found in the public. His media-blend note asks for temporal weighting and does not cover platform selection or how silence is scored. That note is not stale, but it is incomplete on this point. Nothing here contradicts his takeaways.

Item exists. Paul's annotations on it include a highlight reading more network data is not always better (highlight only, no note). That supports the caution, but the wording is network data, not layers. Kept with corrected wording.
Item exists; title matches. Its extracted summary says the criterion came from ordinary users of Facebook, Twitter, Weibo and Instagram, so the frame caveat applies. Kept.

Item exists. The paper concedes a non-representative Santiago news-follower sample (Sec. 3.2, Sec. 5.1 p.12, Sec. 6.1 p.16), and Hargittai is relevant to such biases. The paper does not cite her, so 'explains' should read 'relevant to'.

Read together, this limits how far its findings by income can be trusted.

meta.title: How to train your stochastic parrot: large language models for political texts
meta.venue: Political Science Research and Methods, vol. 13, pp. 264-281 (Cambridge University Press, open access CC BY 4.0). Received 12 Sep 2023, revised 23 Jul 2024, accepted 3 Aug 2024. Authors at University of Georgia (Ornstein, Blasingame) and University of Florida (Truscott).

extraction.title: How to train your stochastic parrot: large language models for political texts
extraction.venue: Political Science Research and Methods, vol. 13, pp. 264-281 (Cambridge University Press, open access CC BY 4.0). Received 12 Sep 2023, revised 23 Jul 2024, accepted 3 Aug 2024. Authors at University of Georgia (Ornstein, Blasingame) and University of Florida (Truscott).
extraction.document_type: Journal article (original article) with pre-registered analyses
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 761 lines of the _text file (about 61.6k chars), including references and the cite block. Paul's markup: none. No file in _annots/ (63 JSON files) references hash 67b4400dd0c4 or the title, and no file in annotations/ mentions Ornstein or the title, so paul_markup is empty. Metadata corrections: the hint DOI (from PII S2049847024000645) does not match the DOI printed in the text, which is 10.1017/psrm.2024.64; the journal is Political Science Research and Methods, not a Cambridge book; the year is 2025 by volume (accepted 2024). Topic coverage: lobbying, network analysis, path-finding, allocation, and persuasion/turnout are absent. Legislators appear only through House floor speeches (virtue-praise labels by party). Elections appear only through campaign-ad tone; no vote, turnout, or persuasion outcome is modeled.
extraction.research_question: Can few-shot prompts to large language models (GPT-3, GPT-4) be adapted, without task-specific training or large labeled sets, to political text-as-data tasks (sentiment classification, ad tone classification, ideology scaling, topic discovery), matching or beating conventional automated methods and approaching expert or crowd coding at far lower cost? The paper also asks what validation and prompt-design practices make such measures trustworthy.
extraction.theory: Text-as-data measurement (Grimmer and Stewart 2013: "validation, validation, validation"). Contextualized word embeddings and transformer self-attention let word meaning depend on context (Vaswani et al. 2017), so context-dependent labels such as sarcasm can be learned from a prompt rather than from a trained classifier. Few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020). For topics, the expectation that conservatives praise loyalty, patriotism and hard work while liberals praise fairness, compassion and charity follows Moral Foundations Theory (Graham et al. 2009), p.275.
extraction.data: Four applications. (1) 945 tweets referencing the US Supreme Court within 24 hours of Masterpiece Cakeshop (2018) and of Trump v. Mazars and Trump v. Vance (2020); unit = tweet; author-coded 7-point sentiment from -1 to +1 after two-stage manual coding (1000 labeled, 55 dropped, 945 kept; Fleiss kappa 0.72). Benchmark classifier trained on 1.2 million tweets from Go et al. (2009). (2) 935 political ads from Carlson and Montgomery (2017); unit = ad; expert ratings and crowd pairwise comparisons (9420 tasks at 6 cents, $565.20 total). (3) 18,263 sentences from 18 British party manifestos, 1987-2010; crowd-coded per Benoit et al. (2016), with an expert-score benchmark. (4) 9,704 one-minute US House floor speeches in the 113th Congress (2013-2014) from Wilkerson and Casas (2017); 9,565 analyzed because 139 speeches over 6,000 characters were omitted for API token limits (fn. 8, p.275). Models: GPT-3 (175B parameters) and GPT-4; GPT-3 was removed from the public API in January 2024 (p.278).
extraction.method: Few-shot prompting. The LLM returns a next-word probability vector over labels, and continuous measures are built from it. Sentiment (tweets): six few-shot examples, two per class (positive, neutral, negative), with a preamble describing the ruling; the continuous measure is the first principal component of the probability vector (pre-registered via AsPredicted 92341, 92422, 92666, 100718, 125217; p.267-268). Ad tone: one-shot prompt (Figure 3), continuous tone from the probability vector. Ideology: one-shot Policy Prompt applied per sentence; sentence score = P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal); averaged to economic and social passage means per manifesto (p.273). GPT-4 ideology deviated from the pre-registered protocol and used the Le Mens and Gallego (2023) whole-document prompt (p.273). Topics: prompt asks GPT-3 for virtue labels; 51,483 labels returned, about 5-6 per speech, grouped by synonyms (p.275-276). Benchmarks: dictionary sentiment, Naive Bayes (bag of words), TweetNLP (RoBERTa fine-tuned on tweets, Camacho-Collados et al. 2022). Appendix A has zero-shot and one-shot variants (not in the text file).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is measurement validation: each LLM measure is correlated with or compared against human gold labels (author codes, expert ratings, crowd codes), and topic labels are validated by an optimal-label task in which a blinded coder picks the best of four labels for 400 speeches (80 percent agreed with GPT-3's label, chance 25 percent; p.276).
extraction.scope: Population and era: US tweets about SCOTUS decisions (2018-2020); US campaign ads from the Carlson and Montgomery (2017) corpus (dates not stated in text); UK party manifestos 1987-2010; US House one-minute floor speeches 2013-2014. Models: GPT-3 and GPT-4 (2023-2024 API). The paper argues about political science text-as-data generally, and cautions about closed proprietary models and about tasks needing current or factual information (p.278-279).

key_findings.finding: Sentiment on 945 SCOTUS tweets: GPT-3 few-shot correctly predicts negative/positive in 88.4 percent of cases; TweetNLP 64.3 percent; best dictionary method 38.3 percent; Naive Bayes trained on 1.2M tweets 57.7 percent.

GPT-4 performs slightly worse than GPT-3 on the sentiment task; its probabilities are poorly calibrated and overconfident; for over 70 percent of posts GPT-4 gives a single-label probability above 99 percent; it returns Neutral more often than the authors.
key_findings.numbers: over 70% of posts with >99% probability

key_findings.finding: Ad tone: LLM coding of 935 ads took under one minute and cost $0.60, against $565.20 for crowd pairwise coding (9420 tasks at 6 cents), about a 1000-fold cost reduction. The LLM tone measure is said to correlate with expert ratings as strongly as the crowd measure; the text gives no coefficient for this.
key_findings.location: Section 3.2, p.269 (crowd cost lines 326-327) and p.271 (lines 355-358)
key_findings.numbers: $0.60 vs $565.20; 935 ads; under 1 minute

key_findings.finding: Ideology scaling of 18 UK manifestos: LLM scores correlate with expert ratings at rho = 0.92 on the economic dimension and rho = 0.8 on the social dimension; better at between-party than within-party variance (true for crowd codes too).
key_findings.numbers: rho 0.92 economic; rho 0.8 social

key_findings.finding: Cost of ideology scoring: about $2.50 for 18,263 sentences with GPT-3, against about $3,226.70 for the original crowd coding (footnote assumes 1.5 cents per sentence and 215,107 crowd evaluations).
key_findings.numbers: $2.50 vs ~$3226.70; 18,263 sentences; 215,107 evaluations

key_findings.finding: Topic labeling of 9,565 House speeches returned 51,483 labels (about 5-6 per speech). Democrats more often praised advocacy (+3.5 pp), charity (+1.5), compassion (+3.9), education (+3.3), fairness (+3). Republicans more often praised bravery (+2), patriotism (+4.2), loyalty (+2.1), sacrifice (+2.8), success (+7.7).
key_findings.numbers: 51,483 labels; differences in percentage points as listed

key_findings.finding: Topic label validation: for 400 random speeches a blinded coder picked GPT-3's label over three random intruders in 80 percent of cases, against 25 percent chance.
key_findings.numbers: 80% vs 25% chance; n = 400

key_findings.finding: The model is not a dictionary method: 5,332 speeches contain the word honor, but GPT-3 labels only 145 as praising honor, nearly all about soldiers or veterans.
key_findings.numbers: 5,332 contain honor; 145 labeled as praising honor

key_findings.finding: Cost trend: computing cost of the paper's applications fell 97 percent between fall 2021 and publication.
key_findings.numbers: 97% decline

key_findings.finding: Reproducibility: GPT-3 models used were removed from the public API in January 2024, so exact results cannot be reproduced unless the weights are released.
key_findings.numbers: January 2024

key_findings.finding: Bias: GPT-3 answered 58 percent of 817 misconception questions truthfully (Lin et al. 2021), cited as a reason for caution on factual-accuracy tasks.

limitations: Results depend on researcher choices, especially prompt design; the authors recommend a three-step validation: hand-label a small set for prompt design, validate on a second hand-labeled set, then apply to the rest (p.277, lines 567-575).
GPT-4 is worse-calibrated than GPT-3 for next-word classification because of RLHF (p.268, lines 293-296; p.278, lines 587-597).
Reproducibility depends on proprietary, closed models that vendors may stop serving; the GPT-3 models used were retired from the API (p.278).
LLMs inherit human biases and falsehoods, including stereotyped embeddings, and can generate hate speech; RLHF mitigates this at some cost to accuracy (p.278, lines 611-624).
Authors advise against tasks that need up-to-date factual information (p.278-279).
Ad tone: model diverges from experts on attacks against unnamed targets, and on ads needing outside context; the authors argue one expert label is arguably miscoded (p.271, lines 359-368).
Sentiment: tweets whose meaning depends on outside political context can be misread unless the prompt supplies that context.
Pre-registration deviation: GPT-4 ideology used a different, non-pre-registered protocol (p.273, lines 433-440).
Speeches over 6,000 characters (139) were dropped because of API token limits (p.275, fn. 8).
Topic labels are checked only by the 400-speech intruder task; the LDA comparison is conceptual and cited, not estimated in this paper.
GPT-4 showed little or no improvement over GPT-3 on the ideology and sentiment tasks, so the best-model choice is not settled across tasks (p.273, lines 438-440).
measures: Sentiment: first principal component of the Positive/Negative/Neutral next-word probability vector per tweet, compared with a 7-point author-coded score from -1 to +1 (Fleiss kappa 0.72).
Tone: continuous score from the one-shot ad-tone prompt probability vector, compared with expert ratings of the 935 ads.
Ideology: per-sentence score P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal), averaged to economic and social passage means per manifesto; compared with expert scores (rho 0.92 economic, 0.8 social).
Topic: count and share of speeches mentioning each virtue label (and synonyms), by party; difference in percentage points.
Classification accuracy: share of tweets whose predicted negative/positive sign matches the author label (88.4% for GPT-3).
Calibration: share of posts with a single-label probability above 99 percent (GPT-4).

summary_md:
Ornstein, Blasingame and Truscott (PSRM 2025, DOI 10.1017/psrm.2024.64) test few-shot prompts to GPT-3 and GPT-4 on four political text tasks. The tasks are sentiment in 945 SCOTUS tweets, tone in 935 campaign ads, ideology in 18,263 sentences from UK manifestos, and virtue-topic labels for 9,565 House one-minute speeches. On the tweets, GPT-3 got 88.4% of negative/positive signs right, against 64.3% for TweetNLP, 57.7% for Naive Bayes and 38.3% for the best dictionary. On ideology, LLM scores correlate with expert scores at rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across the 18 manifestos. LLM topic labels beat three random intruders in 80% of 400 blinded checks, where chance is 25%. Costs dropped about 1000-fold compared with crowd coding.

Three method points matter more than the headline numbers:
- Continuous measures are built from the label probability vector, not the argmax label.
- GPT-4, tuned with human feedback (RLHF), is overconfident. For over 70% of posts it put more than 99% on one label, and it chose Neutral more often than the human coders.
- Validation runs in three steps: tune the prompt on one hand-labelled set, check it on a second, then apply.

The authors also warn that the GPT-3 models they used were retired in January 2024, so the results cannot be reproduced.

extraction.title: Competitive Influence Maximization in Voter Dynamics
extraction.year: Not printed in the text (metadata hint says 2025; latest cited reference is 2024, Palermo et al.)
extraction.venue: Preprint submitted to Elsevier (29 pages). No journal named in the text. Affiliations: Xiamen University of Technology (Cai); University of Southampton (Gerding, Brede).
extraction.document_type: Preprint manuscript (simulation and mean-field analysis; not empirical)
extraction.coverage: Read all 2506 lines of the text file in three chunks (lines 1-955, 956-1755, 1756-2506), covering abstract, introduction, Sections 2-5, Appendices A-E, acknowledgements and references. Nothing omitted. Paul markup: none supplied (the task listed no markup files), so paul_markup is empty. Coverage is complete for the text as extracted; figure content is read only from axis labels and captions.
extraction.research_question: How do the timing and distribution of a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign shape the final vote share in a voter model, and how does network degree heterogeneity change the optimal campaign timing? Two settings: (1) one controller (A) against a constant, fixed opponent (B); (2) two controllers choosing start times simultaneously in a zero-sum game (paper Sections 1, 2, abstract p.1).
extraction.theory: Non-progressive voter model (reversible opinion changes; Masuda 2015) with heterogeneous mean-field theory and relaxation-time analysis (Son et al. 2008). Degree heterogeneity drives timescales. Competitive timing and budget allocation are analysed with interior-point optimization, stochastic hill climbing, and minimax-based iterative search for Nash equilibria in a zero-sum game. Partial zealotry (Masuda et al. 2010; Moreno et al. 2020) adds agent heterogeneity. Authors contrast their smooth zealotry with latency models (Palermo et al. 2024).
extraction.data:
Simulated and real networks, no empirical opinion or vote-outcome data.
(a) Synthetic configuration-model scale-free networks. Main experiments: N = 10^4 nodes, target mean degree 10 (realized 10.5), degree exponent lambda in [1.6, 5], k_max = sqrt(N) (p.11, p.25). Individual-optimization experiments: N = 10^2, mean degree 6, k_max = 30, 10 realizations (p.17, p.25). Complete-network zealotry experiment: N = 10^2 (p.26). Each figure reports 100 or 10 realizations (see captions).
(b) Real networks, Table 1 (p.11): Congress votes N=219, 764 edges, mean degree 7.0, lambda about 1.9 (text: mentions between US politicians with supportive or opposing edges). Facebook N=3862, 87324 edges, mean degree 45.2, lambda about 1.6 (users affiliated with one corporation). Advogato N=6541, 51127 edges, mean degree 15.6, lambda about 1.7 (trust network). Wikipedia Elections N=7118, 103689 edges, mean degree 29.1, lambda about 1.5 (positive/negative votes between users; these are Wikipedia admin-style votes, not political elections). Twitter N=22322, 31823 edges, mean degree 2.9, lambda about 4.3 (following network).
Unit of analysis: individual node (agent). Time: simulated horizons T=16 (short) and T=256 (long), dimensionless model time, not calendar periods. Initial opinion share 0.5 for all nodes (or 0 in some experiments, p.18, p.26); one illustrative example uses S_A(0)=0.55 with N=10^4, T=30 (p.5).
extraction.method:
Analytical plus numerical simulation.
- Model (Eq. 1, p.4): each node's opinion-A probability x_i(t) evolves under neighbour influence and two controllers with time-varying gains a_i(t), b_i(t). Budget constraints sum of integrals <= b_A, b_B (p.3-4). Vote share S_A(T) = mean of x_i(T) (Eq. 2).
- Constant-opponent, uniform start (Sec 2.1, Eq. 3-5): A's gain is 0 until t_a, then b_A/((T-t_a)N); B's gain is constant b_B/(TN). Optimal t_a solved by interior-point method (p.5).
- Individual optimization (Sec 2.2, Eq. 6-7): each node has its own start time and budget; stochastic hill climbing (Algorithm 1, p.7), with L_max = N^2 iterations (p.26). Budget moves between nodes keep the total fixed.
- Heterogeneity extension (Sec 2.2.1, Eq. 8): partial zealots with probability q_i of resisting adoption of A when holding B.
- Game (Sec 2.3, Eq. 9; Algorithm 2, p.8): simultaneous choice of start times t_a, t_b; iterative alternating best responses (A maximizes, B minimizes S_A(T)) with step size mu = 1/i, stopping threshold 1e-9 (p.8).
- Mean-field (Sec 3, Eq. 10-11, derived in App. B): nodes grouped by degree k; closed-form x_k(t) and S_A(t).
- Relaxation times (Eq. 12-14, 19): normalized order parameter r_k(t); tau_relax,k and tau_relax as degree-weighted averages; l-percentage relaxation time tau^l.
- Taylor expansion (Eq. 15-18) to second order in 1/k, assuming (a_k+b_k)/k << 1.
- Numerical integration: 4th-order Runge-Kutta, time step 0.01 (p.11).
- Real-network experiments: Table 2 compares optimized t_a with t_a=0 at T in {16, 256} and b_A/b_B in {0.1, 1, 10}.
- Appendix A: single-node case with fully flexible allocation via calculus of variations (Eq. 20-30), yielding a transcendental equation for start time.
extraction.identification: None in a causal sense; model-based simulation. Mean-field and Taylor predictions are validated against Runge-Kutta integration (Fig. 2, 3, 4c-f; p.11-16). Optimality of the start time is checked by a convex vote-share peak (Fig. 4c-d, p.15-16). Within-model comparison is optimized start versus t_a=0 (Table 2, p.18).
extraction.scope: Population: abstract simulated networks (configuration model) and five public network datasets; no sampled human population. Era: none stated. Opinions: binary (A or B), simple contagion, unit link weights, complete knowledge of network topology assumed (p.22-23). Applications named as motivation only (marketing, politics, public health; p.1-2, p.22); no application-specific calibration or validation is reported.

key_findings.finding: Network heterogeneity shifts optimal timing with horizon. For short horizons, highly heterogeneous networks (low lambda) should start later; for long horizons they should start earlier.
key_findings.location: Sec 4.3.1, p.16-17; Sec 1 p.3 (main finding i)

limitations: Binary opinions and simple contagion only; complex contagion and multi-state opinion models are not studied (p.22).
Assumes complete knowledge of network topology and of the opponent's strategy; partial visibility and uncertain opponent behaviour are flagged as future work (p.22-23).

Mean-field analysis assumes degree-uncorrelated networks (p.9); its accuracy is validated only on configuration-model networks and not on the five real datasets (no mean-field check reported for Table 2).
Taylor expansion valid only when (a_k+b_k)/k is small (p.10).
Individual optimization restricted to N=10^2 for computational reasons; absolute improvements described as very small (p.17-18).

Stochastic hill climbing and the iterative Nash algorithm are numerical heuristics; the text reports no optimality guarantee (p.7-8). Nash equilibria are approximated, not solved in closed form (p.8).
Individual optimization is not analysed in the game-theoretic setting because gains are small (p.22).
Integer k_min forces realized mean degree to deviate from target (target 10 gives 10.5) (p.25).
Degree exponent lower bound 1.6 chosen because lower values fail the k_min constraint (p.25).

Real datasets are not election outcome or lobbying data: Congress votes are mentions/support-oppose edges, Wikipedia Elections are user-to-user votes, Facebook and Twitter are social graphs. No validation against observed vote shares is reported.
Time horizons are abstract model units; no calendar mapping is given beyond the illustrative 30-day example (p.5).

summary_md:
Cai, Gerding and Brede study a time-limited, budget-constrained influence campaign in a non-progressive voter model, where opinions can flip back. They use heterogeneous mean-field theory, relaxation-time analysis, hill climbing and an iterative minimax search for Nash start times. Every result is a simulation on configuration-model scale-free graphs or on five public graphs. The paper uses no observed votes, lobbying or money data.

Findings. Against a fixed opponent, the best strategy is to hold budget back and spend it late. Across all datasets, horizons and budget ratios in Table 2, an optimized start beat starting at t=0. One example is the 'Congress votes' mentions graph at T=16 with equal budgets: vote share 0.705 against 0.500. A richer controller starts earlier: on that graph the optimal start falls from 14.73 at budget ratio 0.1 to 10.48 at ratio 10. High-degree nodes take longer to settle, so on a short horizon the outcome stays far from equilibrium (degree of equilibrium never above 0.82 at T=16). In the two-controller game the side with more budget moves first, and the second mover can only offset its lead, not overtake it. Small budgets go to low-degree nodes. Partial zealots get fewer resources than normal agents.

Why it matters here. Melange's money engines have no time dimension at all. The flip model's pflip = a/(a+b) is a stationary share ratio with no time term, the optimizer allocates dollars with no timing, and the competitive cascades let a member who has been reached stay that colour. The paper is the clearest formal case in the vault that timing and reversibility change who wins under a fixed budget. Its evidence is abstract: model time units, unit edge weights, full knowledge of the network, and no calibration to any real campaign. Read it as a design critique and a source of hypotheses. It does not validate or refute any Melange constant, and any agent analysis built on it stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Vote share at a finite horizon depends on when each controller starts and on degree heterogeneity. At T=16 (dimensionless model time, unit-weight graphs) the degree of equilibrium l never exceeds 0.82 and high-degree nodes relax more slowly. An optimized start beats t_a=0 in all 30 rows of Table 2 (5 real networks, T in {16, 256}, budget ratio in {0.1, 1, 10}). Congress votes network, T=16, budget ratio 1: S_A 0.705 vs 0.500 (model output, not observed votes).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2 p.11-16 (text around Fig 4e); Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), where a and b are each a saturating money pull plus a party-weighted proximity term. It is a static, time-free share with no horizon, no start time and no relaxation lag.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Structural parallel only: both are ratios of competing pulls. Magnitudes do not transfer, since paper time is dimensionless, edges have unit weight and opinions are binary simple contagion. The paper shows that an equilibrium-share form omits timing, not that pflip is miscalibrated.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 2 (30 rows) and text lines 1385-1410 checked; every optimized vote share exceeds its t_a=0 baseline. The pflip formula and docstring match the code. Claim holds. Any quoted figure should name the window (T, dimensionless) and denominator (N=10^4 synthetic; N for Table 1 real networks).

bearings.paper_claim: With the budget fixed, choosing a start time raises final vote share over spending from t=0 (Table 2, constant-opponent setting). For N=100 networks, per-node start times and budgets raise vote share further: the relative gain is large at small budget ratios but small in absolute terms (Fig 6a relative axis 1.00 to 1.25). A resource-limited controller starts later and a resource-rich one starts earlier (abstract; Sec 4.3.1). Under the uniform-start formula (Eq 3-5) the controller spends its budget over a short late window; the paper does not prescribe this as a rule.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Sec 2.1 Eq 3-5 p.4-5; Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18; Sec 4.3.2 Fig 6 p.17-18
bearings.system_side: optimize.py docstring describes a lazy greedy allocator with a Golovin-Krause bound kept as a diagnostic. Defaults are a 2.5M pot in 500 increments with a 10k per-candidate cap (PMAX). It allocates amounts per member with no start time or spending schedule; the objective is time-free winnability.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only as a hypothesis. PAC dollars cannot be withdrawn, FEC per-cycle limits bind, and the paper's continuous gain a_i(t) has no clear counterpart in lump-sum contributions. The paper's large relative gain at small budgets means the per-node result should not be read as uniformly small. Untested on legislators.
bearings.verifier_note: Core claims hold (Table 2, Fig 6 axis labels, abstract). The rewrite adds the large relative gain at small budget ratios, which the bearing omitted. The spend-near-deadline wording is a reading of Eq 3-5, not a paper statement. The name CELF does not appear in the docstring; the code is described as lazy greedy. Appendix A Eq 30 was not re-derived.

bearings.paper_claim: Two settings are mixed here. The optimal start for Congress votes at T=16 falls from 14.730 at budget ratio 0.1 to 10.476 at ratio 10 (Table 2, constant-opponent setting, fixed opponent starting at 0). In the two-controller Nash game the controller with the larger budget moves first, and the second mover can only buffer the first mover's gain, never exceed its vote share (Sec 4.3.4, stage 3, p.21-22). Fig 9b shows per-node resource per unit time rising with the budget advantage.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.3.1 Table 2 p.18; Sec 4.3.4 Fig 8-9 p.19-22
bearings.system_side: The head-to-head panel solves CU share against competitor share in closed form for the baseline odds. It reports that CU money alone cannot fully offset when the required money ratio q is at least 1. The solve uses the CU-to-competitor money ratio at one instant, with no sequencing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's statement that a disadvantaged controller can offset but not overtake agrees in spirit with the cannot-offset message. The claim that a disadvantaged side does better by delaying has no counterpart in a static break-even, and it rests on the paper's abstract and simulations only. Transfer would need a model of within-cycle spending order, which the system lacks.
bearings.verifier_note: The 14.730, 10.476, 0.705 and 0.500 values match Table 2, but Table 2 is the constant-opponent setting, not the game; the original bearing attributed them to the game. The game statement is qualitative. The code description checks out. Fig 9b per-node axis values were not verified against the figure image.

bearings.paper_claim: Competitive influence is analysed in a non-progressive voter model with reversible opinions, where the opponent is a strategic controller choosing its own start time at a Nash equilibrium (Eq 9, Algorithm 2 p.8; Fig 8 p.19-20). The paper does not state that the second mover concentrates its budget in the final stage. Its text says the second mover starts later and can only buffer the first mover's gain (p.21). End-loaded budgets appear for the budget-advantaged controller when the degree exponent is below about 2.2 (Sec 4.3.4, p.21-22).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 2.3 Eq 9 Algorithm 2 p.8; Sec 4.3.4 Fig 8-9 p.19-22
bearings.system_side: A two-colour first-to-reach independent cascade: a reached member keeps its colour for the rest of the run. Industry money enters only as non-strategic bystander activation, min(0.9, ind/400000). Nothing represents an opponent that responds in time.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a difference in model class, not evidence that the independent cascade choice is wrong. The original claims that cosponsorship is close to progressive with rare withdrawals, and that stance and votes are not, have no source in the paper or the code. Those claims are UNVERIFIED here and should not be relied on.
bearings.verifier_note: The model description and the bystander activation formula match the code (BSCALE=400000 in budget_frontier; PB uses the same min with 0.9). The late-countermove claim is not in the paper, so the bearing was rewritten to the paper's actual statements. The cosponsorship assertion is analyst opinion with no citation.

bearings.paper_claim: In the individual-optimization runs with 20 percent of agents as partial zealots (Sec 4.3.3, N=100 per the Sec 4.3.2 reduction; N not restated in 4.3.3), normal agents receive more budget than zealots at every zealotry level q tested. At q=0.1 the maximum zealot allocation is under 20 and the normal-agent maximum is near 25 (allocation units as plotted in Fig 7). At medium and large q zealots get fewer resources and start later as degree rises.

bearings.system_side: PERS in moneyball_core.py gives Opponent 0.08, Highly Skeptical 0.15 and Champion 0.10, with middle tiers between 0.50 and 0.65. The F1 gate in optimize.py gives zero allocation to members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent.

Champion is a committed pro tier, so its low multiplier reflects being already won, not zealot resistance, and it does not support the paper's result. The paper never sets zealot allocation to zero, so it does not support the hard zero gate on its own. Simulated agents only.

bearings.paper_claim: Under node-specific optimization on N=100 networks with mean degree 6 (Sec 4.3.2), the budget ratio sets the degree pattern. With small budget ratios, control gains fall and start times rise with degree, so low-degree nodes are targeted. With large ratios the pattern reverses (Fig 6b-c p.18; Appendix D Fig 10 p.26).

bearings.system_side: The coalition water-fill boosts each candidate's marginal spread by (1 + 0.8 bpf), where bpf is a bipartisan share read from bipartisan.json divided by 100, so it favours bipartisan bridges. The ranking does not depend on budget size, although the CAP-clipped water-fill decides how far down the list money goes.

Measuring the Melange cosponsor graph's degree exponent and testing whether greedy seeds move toward low-degree members at small budgets would be new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED.

summary_issues: Several related links are not in the paper and were dropped: Borodin (no citation, and the paper has no submodularity or greedy-guarantee discussion, so the claim that Cai's timing game shows competition breaks greedy guarantees is false for this paper), Golovin-Krause, Chen 2021 contingency-aware IM and Noble 2024. These are analyst analogies, not paper claims.

Brede, Restocchi and Stein 2019 (ref 10, Effects of time horizons on influence maximization in the voter dynamics) is described by the paper as the most directly relevant prior work, but no item for it exists in the items folder. It should be added as a related link once an item exists.

paul_alignment cites a Kim J. 2025 margin note and Paul's positions on joint-optimizer and competitive-cascade-crn, yet the same paragraph says Paul has not annotated the paper, and the item file has paul_entries empty with no markup supplied. Those statements are unsourced and should be removed or sourced.
Summary findings give 14.73 to 10.48 and 0.705 vs 0.500 without naming the setting; they are constant-opponent Table 2 values, not Nash-game values. The bearing on break-even had this error.

The 0.705 vs 0.500 example and the zealot allocation figures (under 20, near 25) are given without N or time window in the summary, which breaks the rule that every figure names its window and denominator.
The summary's claim that this is the clearest formal case in the vault for timing and reversibility is a vault-level comparison that was not verified here.
The gap about the optimizer uses the name CELF in the bearing, but optimize.py describes lazy greedy; the name should match the code.
Figure-axis values (Fig 6a 1.00 to 1.25; Fig 9b 1 to 3.5) were checked only against text extraction of axis labels, not against the figure images, which cannot be rendered on this machine.
gaps_exposed: No time dimension in any money or influence engine. optimize.py, flip_model.py, budget_frontier.py and scenario.py allocate amounts with no start time, horizon or spending schedule, although the paper shows timing alone shifts final share under a fixed budget.

No model of a strategic opponent. Competitor money is a fixed input or bystander noise (min(0.9, ind/400000)), never a best-responding player, so the system cannot represent a late countermove by banks.

No reversibility. Competitive cascades are first-to-reach and absorbing, while stance in the paper (and in reality) can revert. stance_dynamics measures trajectories, but the allocators do not consume them.
The degree heterogeneity (degree exponent) of the cosponsor graph is unmeasured, though the paper makes optimal timing and degree targeting depend on it, with a regime change near lambda 2.2.

The contested-bills registry has a schema for a counterparty but no consumer, so the paper's two-controller game framing has nowhere to land (fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py:1-20 says no consumer exists).
flags: The paper's 'Congress votes' dataset is a network of mentions between politicians with support/oppose edges. It is not roll calls or cosponsorship, and Table 2 'vote share' is model output, not observed votes. Never quote 0.705 vs 0.500 as an electoral or legislative effect.
'Influence' in the paper is a model-internal controller gain. Under D-025, no bearing here may be read as closeness, access or a probability of moving a member.
Every number in the paper is in dimensionless model time on unit-weight graphs. Any figure carried over must name that window and denominator (N, mean degree, lambda, T, realizations).
The paper does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization; it uses unit weights as a simplification. Neither rejected SNA proposal is implicated.
A degree-exponent measurement or timing test on Melange graphs would be new agent analysis. It stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The component list says contested-bills cites Romero Moreno 2021, but fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py contains no such citation. The link lives only in notes.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It speaks most directly to two of his positions. On competitive-cascade-crn, he wants rival industries modelled and scenarios simulated cheaply. The paper supports the first and goes further: a rival should be a strategic, time-aware player, which the system does not have. On joint-optimizer, he sees adaptive greedy plus CELF as the operational layer and expects learned policies to replace it at scale. The paper adds a missing axis, when to spend, that neither greedy nor GCOMB covers as built. His Kim J. 2025 margin note about conflicting industries is consistent with the two-controller game. His notes are not stale here; the system simply has no timing layer for them to describe. His ROI enthusiasm should be tempered by the paper's own result that per-node fine-tuning yields very small absolute gains.
